study.title: Isaiah 51 Consolation to God's people and judgment upon the oppressors
study.overview: Isaiah 51 presents a word of consolation and steadfastness for the people who seek the LORD in the midst of humiliation and captivity. The chapter calls the listeners to look at the humble origins of Abraham and Sarah, to remember that God's salvation is more stable than the visible world, and to trust that the arm of the LORD will act again as it acted in the past. At the same time, the text denounces the weakness of the oppressors and announces that the cup of wrath will pass from the hands of Zion to the hands of those who afflicted it.

outline.title: Look at the origins and expect restoration
outline.explanation: Those who follow righteousness are called to consider Abraham and Sarah, examples of how God can multiply and restore what seemed small and unlikely. The promise culminates in comfort to Zion, which will return to joy, gratitude and songs.

outline.title: The righteousness and salvation of God are permanent
outline.explanation: God speaks as a source of instruction, judgment, and salvation for the peoples. Though the heavens and the earth pass, the righteousness of the LORD and his salvation remain forever, so the people must not fear human insults that are transitory.

outline.title: The people ask for the intervention of the arm of the LORD
outline.explanation: Prayer and memory unite: the people ask that God act as in the past, crushing evil and paving the way for the redeemed. In response, God presents himself as the Comforter and reaffirms his presence, his words and his creative and ruler power.

outline.title: Jerusalem wakes up, drank the cup and now sees change
outline.explanation: Jerusalem is called to awaken because he suffered the cup of wrath and was left without direction and without strength. But God declares that he will remove this cup from his hand and put it into the hands of the oppressors, reversing the humiliation suffered.

study.context: The notes provided relate this chapter to the situation of a people in distress, probably support for the captives in Babylon, although this is not presented as absolute certainty. The text repeatedly speaks of oppression, destruction, war and hunger, which combines with a scenario of national desolation and the need for spiritual encouragement.
study.theology: The chapter affirms the faithfulness of the God of the covenant, which does not abandon his people or lets his promise fail. Divine salvation is presented as more lasting than present and more reliable creation than any human power. The righteousness of God is not only a moral pattern, but a saving and judging action that brings comfort to the faithful and fall to the oppressors. There is also strong emphasis on memory: remembering the redeeming past strengthens faith in the present. When the text speaks of the arm of the LORD, the notes understand him as God's own power acting decisively; in evangelical Christian reading, this can be read as the language of God's sovereign action to liberate and rule, without forcing the text beyond what he says.

scholarViews.insight: The chapter is organized into three calls to listening, and the first connects the "rocha" and the "excavation of the well" to Abraham and Sarah, that is, to the humble origins of God's people.
Verses 4 to 6 point out that God's righteousness and salvation are firm and very close, therefore they belong to the comfort of God's people.
In verse 6, the eternal duration of God's salvation is presented as a contrast to the transience of the world and of men.

questions: What does it mean, in practice, to look at the origins of Abraham and Sarah when the current situation seems impossible?
How can we trust in God's righteousness and salvation when human insults and pressures seem stronger than faith?
How can the remembrance of God's past acts strengthen hope today?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to exchange despair for memory and trust. Identify what oppression or fear has dominated your heart and bring it to God in prayer, asking him to reaffirm his faithfulness. Then concretely recall two actions of God in his life or in the biblical story that show that his arm has not weakened. Also practice hope with God's people: instead of repeating the language of defeat, speak with gratitude and firmness about the salvation that the Lord promises and sustains.
study.uncertainty: The text of the notes does not allow to affirm with total certainty all the historical details of the scenario, although the reference to captivity and the Babylonians is plausible and appears in the notes. It is also not possible to determine, only with these excerpts, all the nuances of each poetic image without extrapolating the chapter itself. The readings of Matthew Henry and Adam Clarke are interpretative and, in some points, devotional; they should be received as comments, not as absolute definitions of the meaning of the text.
